title: Linux System Administration Comprehensive Exam
subject: System Administration and Maintenance (Linux)
summary: Interactive examination covering five lessons: System Administration and Maintenance (Linux) with operating system comparisons, Linux-versus-Windows differences, the kernel, shells and shell prompts; the File System with Linux and Windows file systems, NFS, ZFS, and the Linux directory structure; Linux distributions and their release timeline; desktop environments, package management systems, boot loaders, and installation; and basic commands covering paths, directories, files, users and groups, filters, archiving, utilities, networking, and links.

chapters.title: System Administration and Maintenance (Linux)
chapters.description: Operating system comparison pros and cons, fundamental Linux-versus-Windows differences, mistakes of new Linux users, kernel objectives, kernel functions and management, kernel types, and shell types with their prompts.

questions.question: In the abbreviation LAMP, what does the letter M stand for?
questions.explanation: LAMP stands for Linux, Apache, MySQL, Perl/PHP/Python, so M is MySQL.

questions.question: Which of these stands for the Free Software Foundation?
questions.explanation: FSF is the Free Software Foundation, a supporter of the GNU project.

questions.question: POSIX is an abbreviation for which standard interface?
questions.explanation: POSIX is the Portable Operating System Interface (Single UNIX Specification).

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a Windows con in the reference?
questions.explanation: Virus attacks are listed among Windows cons; the other choices are Mac or Linux cons.

questions.question: Which advantage is attributed to macOS in the reference?
questions.explanation: For Mac, the reference lists fewer virus attacks as one of its pros.

questions.question: What qualification does the reference add after stating Linux needs no anti-virus?
questions.explanation: Linux does not need anti-virus, but the reference adds that no OS is totally secure.

questions.question: According to the reference, what does Linux need in order to execute code?
questions.explanation: Linux needs root privileges to be able to execute codes, as stated in the fundamental differences.

questions.question: How does Linux handle updates according to the reference?
choices: Updates selected software, then restarts if it needs to
Requires a paid subscription for every package update
Updates everything at once, without forced restarts
Delays all updates until the next major version release
questions.explanation: Linux updates everything at once and never restarts without permission, unlike the Windows behavior described.

questions.question: How do Linux and Windows differ in how they represent drives?
choices: Windows uses alphabet letters; Linux uses /dev
Linux uses alphabet letters; Windows uses /dev
Both use mount points for every drive
Both rely on network shares only
questions.explanation: Linux uses /dev for drives while Windows uses alphabet letters, per the reference.

questions.question: Which of these is listed as a mistake made by new Linux users?
choices: Reading the manual pages before installation
Backing up files before partition table changes
Searching Google to find and install software
questions.explanation: Using Google to find software is among the mistakes new Linux users make.

questions.question: Which is one of the five kernel objectives in the reference?
choices: Render the graphical desktop for the end user
Compile application source code into packages
Link user-level applications with the hardware
Store the user's documents and personal settings
questions.explanation: A kernel objective is to establish communication between user-level applications and hardware, plus controlling disk, memory, and task management.

questions.question: Which of the following is something the kernel manages?
questions.explanation: The kernel manages CPU/GPU, memory, I/O devices, resources, devices, system calls, and security and protection.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a kernel function named in the reference?
questions.explanation: Kernel functions include process, memory, device, and file system management plus IPC and scheduling; web server configuration is not one.

questions.question: Which of these is a type of kernel listed in the reference?
questions.explanation: Microkernel is one of the listed kernel types, along with monolithic, hybrid, exo, nano, VM, and embedded kernels.

questions.question: Which kernel type is also referred to as a Virtual Machine (VM) kernel or hypervisor?
questions.explanation: The VM Kernel or Hypervisor is one of the seven kernel types listed.

questions.question: Which shell is the GNU Bourne-Again Shell?
questions.explanation: bash is the GNU Bourne-Again Shell.

questions.question: Which shell is described as the Friendly Interactive Shell?
questions.explanation: fish (or fsh), the Friendly Interactive Shell, is one of the shell types listed.

questions.question: Which prompt character indicates a root user in the Bourne shell?
questions.explanation: The Bourne shell shows # for root and $ for non-root users.

questions.question: What is the non-root prompt in the C shell (csh)?
questions.explanation: The C shell uses # for root and % for non-root users.

questions.question: What is the root prompt in the Z Shell (zsh)?
questions.explanation: The Z Shell shows hostname># for root and hostname>$ for non-root users.

questions.question: SCSI stands for which of the following?
questions.explanation: SCSI is the Small Computer System Interface.

questions.question: ACPI is an abbreviation for which interface standard?
questions.explanation: ACPI is the Advanced Configuration and Power Interface.

questions.question: NUMA stands for which memory architecture?
questions.explanation: NUMA is Non-Uniform Memory Access.

questions.question: What does initramfs stand for?
choices: Initial Random Access Memory File Store
questions.explanation: initramfs is the Initial RAM File System.

questions.question: Btrfs stands for which of the following?
questions.explanation: Btrfs is the B-tree File System.

questions.question: What does the statement 'Linux is yours, Windows is still theirs' mean in the reference?
choices: Windows can only be copied after paying for it
Users control Linux; the vendor owns Windows
Linux belongs to a single software company
Windows cannot be customized or modified at all
questions.explanation: The reference contrasts Linux as user-controlled versus Windows as vendor-controlled software.

questions.question: Which two drawbacks are both listed under the Mac cons in the reference?
choices: Expensive and fewer games and software
questions.explanation: Under Mac cons the reference lists expensive, fewer games and software, and no hardware customization.

questions.question: Which item appears in the Linux pros list in the reference?
choices: A similar GUI for all products
questions.explanation: The Linux pros include open-source, no anti-virus need, powerful CLI, low specs, multitasking, and less disk space.

questions.question: Which kernel function deals with communication between running processes?
questions.explanation: Inter-Process Communication (IPC) is a kernel function that handles process communication.

questions.question: What does SELinux stand for?
questions.explanation: SELinux is Security-Enhanced Linux.

chapters.title: File System
chapters.description: File system abbreviations, Linux and Microsoft Windows file systems, ZFS use cases, NFS components, and the Linux directory structure under the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard.

questions.question: Which abbreviation stands for Filesystem Hierarchy Standard?
questions.explanation: FHS is the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard that defines Linux directory locations.

questions.question: What does COW stand for in file system terms?
questions.explanation: COW stands for Copy-on-Write.

questions.question: Which of these is listed as a Linux file system in the reference?
questions.explanation: Btrfs is listed among Linux file systems, while NTFS, exFAT, and ReFS are Windows file systems.

questions.question: What does the abbreviation XFS stand for?
questions.explanation: XFS stands for X File System.

questions.question: What does ZFS stand for?
questions.explanation: ZFS stands for Zettabyte File System.

questions.question: What does exFAT stand for?
questions.explanation: exFAT is the Extended File Allocation Table.

questions.question: What does NTFS stand for?
questions.explanation: NTFS is the New Technology File System.

questions.question: What does ReFS stand for?
questions.explanation: ReFS is the Resilient File System.

questions.question: What are the two components of NFS named in the reference?
questions.explanation: The components of NFS are the NFS Server and the NFS Client.

questions.question: Which of these is listed as a common use case for ZFS?
questions.explanation: ZFS use cases include Enterprise Storage Solutions, Backup and Disaster Recovery, and File Server and NAS.

questions.question: Which of these is a Microsoft Windows file system in the reference?
questions.explanation: MS Windows file systems are FAT, NTFS, exFAT, Live File System, and ReFS.

questions.question: Which Linux directory holds host-specific system-wide configuration files?
questions.explanation: /etc holds host-specific system-wide configuration files.

questions.question: Which directory contains user home directories?
questions.explanation: /home contains user home directories.

questions.question: Which directory contains device files?
questions.explanation: /dev is the device files directory.

questions.question: Which directory is a virtual filesystem for process and kernel information?
questions.explanation: /proc is the virtual filesystem for process and kernel information.

questions.question: Which directory stores variable data files?
questions.explanation: /var holds variable data files.

questions.question: Which directory is intended for temporary files?
questions.explanation: /tmp is the temporary files directory.

questions.question: Which directory is the secondary hierarchy for user data and applications?
questions.explanation: /usr is the secondary hierarchy for user data and applications.

questions.question: Which directory is the home directory for the root user?
questions.explanation: /root is the home directory for the root user.

questions.question: Which directory provides mount points for removable media?
questions.explanation: /media holds mount points for removable media.

questions.question: Which directory is used for temporarily mounted filesystems?
questions.explanation: /mnt is for temporarily mounted filesystems.

questions.question: Which directory holds essential system administrative binaries?
questions.explanation: /sbin holds essential system administrative binaries.

questions.question: Which directory holds add-on application software packages?
questions.explanation: /opt holds add-on application software packages.

questions.question: Which directory holds site-specific data served by the system?
questions.explanation: /srv holds site-specific data served by the system.

questions.question: Which directory holds run-time variable data?
questions.explanation: /run holds run-time variable data.

questions.question: Which directory holds device, driver, and kernel feature information?
questions.explanation: /sys holds device, driver, and kernel feature information.

questions.question: Which directory holds essential command binaries?
questions.explanation: /bin holds essential command binaries.

questions.question: Which directory holds the boot loader files?
questions.explanation: /boot holds boot loader files.

questions.question: What does the abbreviation USR stand for?
questions.explanation: USR stands for User System Resources.

questions.question: In the Linux directory structure, which of these is the primary root directory written as a single slash?
questions.explanation: The primary root directory of the Linux hierarchy is /.

chapters.title: Linux Distributions
chapters.description: Linux distribution abbreviations and the release timeline of the distributions listed in the reference, from Slackware in July 1993 to Mageia in June 2011.

questions.question: What does YaST stand for?
questions.explanation: YaST is 'Yet another Setup Tool', the configuration tool used by SUSE.

questions.question: What does RHEL stand for?
questions.explanation: RHEL is Red Hat Enterprise Linux.

questions.question: What does KVM stand for?
questions.explanation: KVM is the Kernel-based Virtual Machine.

questions.question: Which distribution in the reference timeline has the earliest release date?
questions.explanation: Slackware, released July 1993, is the earliest listed distribution.

questions.question: Which distribution was released in September 1993?
questions.explanation: Debian was released in September 1993.

questions.question: Which distribution was released in May 1995?
questions.explanation: Red Hat was released in May 1995.

questions.question: Which distribution was released in September 2000?
questions.explanation: Knoppix was released in September 2000.

questions.question: Which two distributions in the reference share the release date of March 2002?
questions.explanation: Both Gentoo and Arch Linux were released in March 2002.

questions.question: Which distribution was released in November 2003?
questions.explanation: Fedora was released in November 2003.

questions.question: Which distribution is recorded in the reference only with the year 2004?
questions.explanation: CentOS is recorded simply as 2004, while Ubuntu has October 2004.

questions.question: Which distribution was released in October 2004?
questions.explanation: Ubuntu was released in October 2004.

questions.question: Which distribution was released in August 2005?
questions.explanation: Alpine Linux was released in August 2005.

questions.question: Which distribution was released in October 2006?
questions.explanation: Oracle Linux was released in October 2006.

questions.question: Which distribution was released in December 2006?
questions.explanation: Musix was released in December 2006.

questions.question: Which distribution was released in September 2008?
questions.explanation: Android was released in September 2008.

questions.question: Which distribution in the reference has the most recent release date?
questions.explanation: Mageia, released June 2011, is the most recent listed distribution.

questions.question: Which distribution was released in 1994?
questions.explanation: SUSE was released in 1994.

questions.question: Which of these distributions appears in the reference timeline?
questions.explanation: Slackware appears in the timeline, while the others are not listed in it.

questions.question: What does the abbreviation DVD stand for?
questions.explanation: DVD stands for Digital Versatile Disc.

questions.question: Which pairing of distribution and release year matches the reference?
questions.explanation: Ubuntu was released in October 2004; Fedora was November 2003, CentOS 2004, and Gentoo March 2002.

chapters.title: Desktop Environments, Package Management, and Boot Loaders
chapters.description: Desktop environments, display renderers, display managers, partitioning utilities, Linux installation steps, package formats and package managers, system installers, and boot loaders with system requirements.

questions.question: What does the abbreviation DE stand for?
questions.explanation: DE stands for Desktop Environment.

questions.question: What does MBR stand for?
questions.explanation: MBR stands for Master Boot Record.

questions.question: What does GPT stand for?
questions.explanation: GPT is the GUID Partition Table.

questions.question: What does GUID stand for?
questions.explanation: GUID stands for Globally Unique Identifier.

questions.question: Which two technologies are named as the major display renderers?
questions.explanation: The major display renderers cited are Xorg / X Window System (X11) and Wayland.

questions.question: Which of these is a common Linux partitioning utility?
questions.explanation: parted, fdisk, gdisk, cfdisk, gparted, and lsblk are the Linux partitioning utilities listed.

questions.question: Which display manager expands to GNOME Display Manager?
questions.explanation: GDM (or GDM3) is the GNOME Display Manager.

questions.question: Which display manager is the Simple Desktop Display Manager?
questions.explanation: SDDM stands for Simple Desktop Display Manager.

questions.question: Which display manager is described as Lightweight?
questions.explanation: LightDM is the Lightweight Display Manager; Ly is also described as Lightweight.

questions.question: Which of these is listed as a Linux desktop environment?
questions.explanation: KDE Plasma, GNOME, XFCE, LXDE, and LXQt are among the desktop environments listed.

questions.question: Which sequence matches the Linux installation steps given in the reference?
choices: Partition, Keyboard settings, User Information, Set Timezone, Install files
Keyboard settings, Partition, Set Timezone, User Information, Install files
Set Timezone, Keyboard settings, Partition, Install files, User Information
User Information, Set Timezone, Keyboard settings, Partition, Install files
questions.explanation: The reference order is Keyboard settings, Partition, Set Timezone, User Information, then Install files.

questions.question: Which package format is used by Gentoo Linux?
questions.explanation: ebuild is the Gentoo Linux package format.

questions.question: Which package format is distribution-agnostic and mainly used by Ubuntu per the reference?
questions.explanation: Snap is distribution-agnostic and mainly associated with Ubuntu.

questions.question: Which package format is .pkg.tar.zst used by?
questions.explanation: .pkg.tar.zst is the package format of Arch Linux.

questions.question: Which package manager belongs to Node.js?
questions.explanation: npm is the Node.js package manager.

questions.question: Which package manager belongs to Python?
questions.explanation: pip is the Python package manager.

questions.question: Which package manager is used by Arch Linux?
questions.explanation: pacman is the Arch Linux package manager.

questions.question: Which package manager is used by openSUSE and SUSE?
questions.explanation: zypper is the package manager for openSUSE / SUSE.

questions.question: Which of these is listed as an RPM mode?
questions.explanation: RPM modes include Query, Verify, Install, Upgrade, Erase, Show querytags, and Show configuration.

questions.question: Which of these is a Linux system installer?
questions.explanation: Anaconda, Debian-Installer, DrakX, Preseed, Snap, Wubi, and Calamares are the system installers listed.

questions.question: Which task is performed by Debian-Installer?
questions.explanation: Debian-Installer detects hardware, installation media, and other OSes, configures the network and APT, and sets up user accounts.

questions.question: Which of these is a boot loader listed in the reference?
questions.explanation: GNU GRUB, LILO, rEFInd, BootX, NTLDR, BURG, and SYSLINUX are the boot loaders listed.

questions.question: Which boot-related program is the Windows Boot Manager?
questions.explanation: BOOTMGR is the Windows Boot Manager; NTLDR is the NT Loader.

questions.question: What does GRUB stand for?
questions.explanation: GRUB is the GRand Unified Bootloader.

questions.question: What does UEFI stand for?
questions.explanation: UEFI is the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface.

questions.question: Which distribution requires 8 GB RAM (12 GB recommended) per the reference?
questions.explanation: Fedora lists 8 GB RAM (12 GB recommended), Ubuntu and SUSE 4 GB, Linux Mint 4 GB+, and Kali 2 GB.

questions.question: Which desktop environment does the abbreviation XFCE stand for?
questions.explanation: XFCE stands for XForms Common Environment.

questions.question: Which window manager is the Binary Space Partitioning Window Manager?
questions.explanation: BSPWM is the Binary Space Partitioning Window Manager.

questions.question: What does XDMCP stand for?
questions.explanation: XDMCP is the X Display Manager Control Protocol.

questions.question: Which of these is a package format consumed by Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Fedora, and CentOS?
questions.explanation: RPM is used by RHEL, Fedora, CentOS, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server, and openSUSE.

chapters.title: Basic Commands
chapters.description: Linux paths, directory and file commands, more command navigation keys, user and group commands, /etc/passwd fields, UID ranges, filter commands, compression tools and tar options, utility commands, networking commands, and link commands.

questions.question: What are the two types of Linux paths?
questions.explanation: Linux paths are either relative or absolute.

questions.question: Which command prints the current working directory?
questions.explanation: pwd prints the working directory.

questions.question: Which command makes a new directory?
questions.explanation: mkdir (make directory) creates a new directory.

questions.question: Which command removes an empty directory?
questions.explanation: rmdir (remove directory) removes an empty directory.

questions.question: Which command creates empty files?
questions.explanation: touch creates empty files.

questions.question: Which command concatenates and displays file content?
questions.explanation: cat concatenates and displays file content.

questions.question: Which command outputs a string?
questions.explanation: echo outputs a string; printf is described as formatted printing.

questions.question: Which command performs formatted printing according to the reference?
questions.explanation: printf is the command for formatted printing.

questions.question: Which command displays the first lines of a file?
questions.explanation: head displays the first lines of a file.

questions.question: Which command displays file contents in reverse order?
questions.explanation: tac displays file contents in reverse order.

questions.question: Which command is described as an enhanced file viewer?
questions.explanation: less is described as the enhanced file viewing command.

questions.question: In the more command, which key scrolls down page by line?
questions.explanation: Enter scrolls down page by line in more.

questions.question: In the more command, which key moves to the previous page?
questions.explanation: The b key moves to the previous page in more.

questions.question: In the more command, which key searches for a string?
questions.explanation: The / key searches for a string in more.

questions.question: Which command switches to the administrative user?
questions.explanation: su switches to the administrative user.

questions.question: Which command displays the UID and GID of a user?
questions.explanation: id displays the UID and GID.

questions.question: Which command adds a user account?
questions.explanation: useradd adds a user account.

questions.question: Which command changes a user's password?
questions.explanation: passwd changes the user password.

questions.question: Which command deletes a user account?
questions.explanation: userdel (or deluser) deletes a user account.

questions.question: Which command modifies an existing user account?
questions.explanation: usermod modifies a user account.

questions.question: Which command creates a user group?
questions.explanation: groupadd creates a user group.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a field in the /etc/passwd file?
questions.explanation: /etc/passwd fields are username, password marker, UID, GID, GECOS info, home directory, and shell; the gateway is not among them.

questions.question: Which UID is reserved for the root user?
questions.explanation: UID 0 is reserved for the root user.

questions.question: Which UID range is reserved for regular user accounts?
questions.explanation: UID 1000 and above is for regular user accounts.

questions.question: Which UID range covers predefined system accounts?
questions.explanation: UID 1-99 is for predefined system accounts; 100-999 covers system accounts and groups.

questions.question: Which of these is a Linux filter command?
questions.explanation: grep, wc, od, and sort are the filter commands listed.

questions.question: Which tar option creates an archive?
questions.explanation: -c creates an archive, -x extracts, -t views content, and -z filters through gzip.

questions.question: Which tar option filters the archive through bzip2?
questions.explanation: -j filters through bzip2 while -z filters through gzip.

questions.question: Which command performs DNS lookups?
questions.explanation: host performs DNS lookups; ping tests connectivity using ICMP.

questions.question: Which command creates a symbolic (soft) link?
questions.explanation: ln -s creates a symbolic/soft link, while link or ln creates a hard link.

encyclopedia.definition: The core of the operating system that establishes communication between user-level applications and hardware, and manages CPU/GPU, memory, I/O devices, resources, devices, system calls, and security and protection.
A software stack abbreviation for Linux, Apache, MySQL, and Perl/PHP/Python.
A recursive acronym for GNU's Not Unix, supported by the Free Software Foundation (FSF).
One of the kernel types listed in the reference, together with microkernel, hybrid, exo kernel, nano kernel, VM kernel or hypervisor, and embedded kernel.
The GNU Bourne-Again Shell; its root prompt is bash-VersionNumber# and its non-root prompt is bash-VersionNumber$.
A kernel function that handles communication between running processes.

The standard that defines the Linux directory structure, such as /etc for configuration, /home for user homes, /dev for device files, /proc for process and kernel information, and /var for variable data.
The Zettabyte File System; common use cases include Enterprise Storage Solutions, Backup and Disaster Recovery, and File Server and NAS.
Network File System, composed of an NFS Server and an NFS Client.
The B-tree File System, listed among the Linux file systems alongside Minix, the ext family, ReiserFS, XFS, ZFS, and JFS.
The Resilient File System, a Microsoft Windows file system.
The earliest distribution in the reference timeline, released in July 1993.
The most recent distribution in the reference timeline, released in June 2011.
Software that provides a graphical login; examples include GDM, SDDM, LightDM, LXDM, XDM, Ly, KDM, WDM, MDM, CDM, SLiM, Entrance, XDMCP, emptty, and greetd.
The RPM Package Manager (originally Red Hat Package Manager), used by Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Fedora, CentOS, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server, and openSUSE.
The GRand Unified Bootloader, one of the boot loaders listed in the reference along with LILO, rEFInd, BootX, NTLDR, BURG, and SYSLINUX.
The Unified Extensible Firmware Interface, which replaces the traditional BIOS-based boot environment.
The command that prints the working directory; a Linux directory command along with mkdir, rmdir, ls, and cd.
A file whose fields are the username, password (x marker), UID, GID, GECOS or user info, home directory, and shell.
Options such as -c (create), -x (extract), -v (verbose), -f (filename), -t (view), -j (bzip2), -z (gzip), -r (append), -W (verify), and -C (extract to a different directory).
UID 0 is the root user, UID 1-99 are predefined system accounts, UID 100-999 are system accounts and groups, and UID 1000 and above are regular user accounts.
